body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Physiotherapist-led mobilisation within 24 hours of hip fracture surgery and length of stay: a randomised trial in two trauma units","authors":"Brennan-Adeyemi C, Solberg-Mwangi T, Okafor-Reyes L","year":2019,"venue":"Morrowvale Orthopaedic Rehabilitation Journal","doi":"10.5555/jor.2019.0336","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomised 260 adults after hip fracture surgery in two trauma units to physiotherapist-led mobilisation within 24 hours or to usual care, in which first mobilisation occurred at a median of 46 hours. Mean length of stay was 13.1 days with early mobilisation and 15.4 days with usual care (difference minus 2.3 days, 95 percent CI minus 4.0 to minus 0.6). Walking ability at 30 days was better in the early group. Patients with severe dementia, postoperative hypotension requiring treatment or delirium at the time of randomisation were excluded, about 30 percent of those screened. Both units provided physiotherapy seven days a week."},{"title":"Early mobilisation and length of stay after hip fracture: a registry analysis adjusting for frailty and delirium","authors":"Kristiansen-Obi H, Delacroix-Mensah A","year":2021,"venue":"Hip Fracture Care Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using a national hip fracture registry, we studied 6,400 patients from 38 hospitals. Patients first mobilised within 24 hours of surgery had a median stay three days shorter than those mobilised later. After adjustment for mobility before the fracture, dementia, American Society of Anesthesiologists grade, delirium and postoperative hypotension, the hazard ratio for discharge was 1.03 (95 percent CI 0.97 to 1.10), indicating no clear difference. The authors argue that sicker patients are mobilised later and stay longer for reasons unrelated to mobilisation, and caution that adjusting for delirium and hypotension after surgery may remove part of a real effect."},{"title":"Mobilisation within 24 or 48 hours of hip fracture surgery and length of stay: a systematic review of nine studies with meta-analysis of four trials","authors":"Harrington-Iwu P, Tanaka-Lindholm S, Mbeki-Castro R","year":2022,"venue":"Rehabilitation Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/rer.2022.0121","providerType":"review","abstract":"We included nine studies of mobilisation within 24 or 48 hours of hip fracture surgery: four randomised trials and five observational studies. In the trials, early mobilisation shortened length of stay (mean difference minus 1.9 days, 95 percent CI minus 3.5 to minus 0.3) with substantial heterogeneity (I squared 64 percent). Observational studies gave inconsistent results, from large reductions to no difference after adjustment. Trials excluded many patients with dementia or delirium, limiting applicability to routine care. The certainty of evidence was rated low."},{"title":"Why patients are not mobilised on the day after hip fracture surgery: reasons documented in physiotherapy notes","authors":"Oduya-Farrell K, Lindgren-Pacheco M","year":2020,"venue":"Quillsby Physiotherapy Letters","doi":"10.5555/pprl.2020.0098","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We read the physiotherapy notes of 310 patients who were not mobilised within 24 hours of hip fracture surgery in three hospitals. Documented reasons were postoperative hypotension in 31 percent, no physiotherapist available at the weekend in 28 percent, delirium or drowsiness in 22 percent, uncontrolled pain in 12 percent and other reasons in 7 percent. Weekend admissions were twice as likely to wait more than 48 hours. The authors note that only the weekend staffing reason is independent of how unwell the patient is."},{"title":"Confounding by indication in studies of early mobilisation: a methodological note","authors":"Achterberg-Silva J, Ruiz-Okonkwo B","year":2023,"venue":"Rehabilitation Methods Notes","doi":"10.5555/rmn.2023.0017","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Observational comparisons of early and late mobilisation are distorted because the reasons for delay also predict long stays. Postoperative hypotension and delirium both delay mobilisation and predict longer stays, yet they may also be partly caused by immobility, so adjusting for them can remove a real effect while not adjusting leaves confounding. We recommend adjusting for characteristics measured before surgery, reporting estimates with and without postoperative conditions, and using reasons for delay that are unrelated to the patient, such as weekend staffing, as a check on confounding."},{"title":"Weekend physiotherapy cover and time to first mobilisation after hip fracture: an interrupted time series","authors":"Hale-Nwosu D, Petrakis-Obi L","year":2018,"venue":"Hip Fracture Care Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"One trauma unit introduced physiotherapy cover on Saturdays and Sundays and compared 18 months before with 18 months after the change. Median time from surgery to first mobilisation fell from 38 to 22 hours, and the proportion mobilised within 24 hours rose from 48 to 71 percent. Mean length of stay fell by 1.1 days, but the confidence interval included no change and a new discharge coordinator started during the same period. The authors conclude that weekend cover reliably speeds mobilisation while its effect on length of stay remains uncertain."},{"title":"Measuring time to first mobilisation from clinical notes: agreement between physiotherapy and nursing entries","authors":"Whitaker-Adeyemi S, Borg-Lindqvist E","year":2024,"venue":"Quillsby Physiotherapy Letters","doi":"10.5555/pprl.2024.0042","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared the time of first mobilisation after hip fracture surgery recorded in physiotherapy entries and in nursing entries for 400 patients. The two sources agreed within two hours for 84 percent of patients. Where they disagreed, the physiotherapy entry usually recorded standing with help while the nursing entry recorded sitting out of bed. Reading one set of paper notes took a median of 22 minutes. We recommend defining first mobilisation as standing or walking with a physiotherapist and using the physiotherapy entry, with the nursing entry as a check."}]}
